title: Himachal Pradesh — Shimla, Kullu, Kasol, Spiti, Kinnaur, Kasauli

places.name: Shimla
places.summary: Himachal's capital and the old British summer capital: the Ridge and Mall, Viceregal Lodge, Jakhoo hill and the UNESCO-listed toy train from Kalka.
places.seoTitle: Shimla Travel Guide: The Ridge, Toy Train & Jakhoo
places.seoDescription: Plan Shimla: the Ridge and Mall, Viceregal Lodge, Jakhoo Temple, the Kalka–Shimla toy train, winter ice skating and how to get there.

images.alt: Christ Church's yellow facade on the Ridge in Shimla
images.caption: Christ Church on the Ridge, Shimla

items.title: Known for
items.body: The Ridge, Mall Road and the toy train

overview.text:
Shimla, the capital of Himachal Pradesh, grew from a small township into the summer capital of British India, and its colonial core still shows it. The Ridge and the Mall remain the town's landmarks, lined by Christ Church, the Gaiety Theatre and Gorton Castle, and the Viceregal Lodge of 1888 now houses the Indian Institute of Advanced Study, with parts open to visitors.

Above the town, Jakhoo Temple stands on Shimla's highest hill at 2,445 m — a half-hour climb from the Ridge, or a ropeway ride. The 96 km Kalka–Shimla railway, opened in 1903 with 102 tunnels, is part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site and is the slow, scenic way up. Shimla also makes a base for the drive into Kinnaur along the Hindustan–Tibet Road.

items.body: Walk the Ridge and the Mall, past Christ Church, the Gaiety Theatre and Scandal Point.
Visit the Viceregal Lodge (1888), now the Indian Institute of Advanced Study.
Climb or take the ropeway to Jakhoo Temple at 2,445 m.
Skate on the open-air ice rink between November and February.
See Chadwick Falls near Summer Hill in the July–September rains.

how_to_reach.text:
By air: daily flights from Delhi land at Jubbarhatti, 23 km from Shimla; Chandigarh is the other option.

By rail: take a broad-gauge train to Kalka, then the narrow-gauge Kalka–Shimla line.

By road: ordinary and luxury coaches run regularly from Delhi and Chandigarh.

best_time.text: Light woollens do from April to October; winter sets in from November and lasts until March, when heavy woollens and jackets are needed. The Summer Festival is held in early June, and the ice-skating season runs until February, with a carnival around Christmas and New Year.

images.caption: The Beas in the Kullu valley

overview.text:
Kullu spreads along the Beas river. Founded as a capital in 1660, it is now the district headquarters and the gateway to Manali, 40 km up the valley.

In October the week-long Kullu Dussehra fills the town as village deities arrive on palanquins. The rest of the year the valley is for the outdoors: rafting on long stretches of the Beas, riverside camping around Raison, and the Great Himalayan National Park — a UNESCO World Heritage Site with no roads inside, home to Himalayan tahr, brown bear, snow leopard and the western tragopan. Manikaran's gurdwara and hot sulphur spring are 45 km away on the Parvati.

how_to_reach.text:
By air: the Kullu–Manali airport at Bhuntar is about 10 km away, with flights to Delhi and Chandigarh.

By road: Kullu is 260 km from Chandigarh and 495 km from Delhi; luxury and ordinary coaches run from Delhi, Chandigarh, Shimla and Dharamshala.

best_time.text: Summer (March–June) is 25–35°C in the valley, the monsoon runs from July to September, and winter (December–February) is 5–15°C with the best chance of snow. Come in October for Dussehra; rafting runs March–May and September–November.

overview.text:
Kasol sits on the banks of the Parvati river between Bhuntar and Manikaran, 36 km from Kullu town. Once a quiet village, it is now split by a bridge into an old and a new township, with a growing number of guesthouses, camps and hotels.

It is a popular stop for backpackers and the usual base for treks to Malana and Kheerganga. The Manikaran gurdwara, with its hot sulphur spring, is just 3.5 km up the valley. There is no railway or airport here — Kasol is reached by road, with regular buses and easy-to-find taxis.

how_to_reach.text:
By air: Bhuntar (Kullu–Manali airport) is about 30 km away.

By road: buses run regularly to Kasol and taxis are easy to hire; there is no rail link.

overview.text:
Spiti — 'the middle land' — is a mountain cold desert of windswept valleys and quiet villages on the Tibet border, lying at well over 3,000 m. Buddhism shapes daily life, and its monasteries are the main draw: Key is 12 km from Kaza, and Tabo's, founded in 996 AD, is the largest monastic complex in the valley.

From Kaza, the main town at about 3,650 m, roads lead to Kibber (18 km), Tabo (48 km), Kunzum Pass (75 km) and Chandratal (98 km). The valley sits in the rain shadow and is pleasant from April to October; in winter it can fall to −20°C. Plan for limited signal — only BSNL works well — and note that foreigners need an Inner Line Permit for some inner areas.

how_to_reach.text:
By road from Manali: regular buses to Kaza run from July to October.

By road from Shimla: buses via Kinnaur run from May to October; sturdy off-road taxis are recommended on both routes.

By air and rail: the nearest airports are Bhuntar and Shimla, and the nearest broad-gauge stations Chandigarh and Kalka — the rest is by road.

best_time.text: Spiti is pleasant from April to October, around 15–20°C in May and June, and stays almost rainless during the monsoon. Winter drops to −20°C. Ladarcha, the big trade fair at Kaza, is held in July/August; Lossar, the New Year, usually falls in February.

overview.text:
Kinnaur lies on the ancient trade route between India and Tibet, its valleys cut by the Sutlej, Spiti and Baspa rivers. It runs from the apple and apricot orchards of the Sangla valley to Chitkul, India's last village on the Tibet border, and from Kalpa — at about 2,960 m, facing Kinner Kailash — to the lake at Nako.

Reckong Peo is the district town: Kalpa is 13 km away, Sangla 38 km, Chitkul 65 km and Nako 102 km. The road in is NH-22, the Hindustan–Tibet Road, and the September Fulaich fair at Sangla and the Tribal Festival at Reckong Peo in late October are the times to see local culture.

how_to_reach.text:
By road: Kinnaur is on NH-22, the Hindustan–Tibet Road; buses and taxis leave from Shimla and Rampur. Reckong Peo is 230 km from Shimla.

By rail and air: the nearest railhead and airport are both at Shimla, 244 km and 267 km away.

items.title: Permits
items.body: Foreign tourists need an Inner Line Permit for some inner areas near the Tibet border.

items.title: Mobile and internet
items.body: Good mobile signal at Reckong Peo, Kalpa and Sangla, but internet can be weak and many trek routes have none.

overview.text:
Kasauli is a small cantonment town in Solan district, set up by the British in 1842 as a hill station, and it keeps much of that unhurried feel. It is about 25–27 km from Solan, 58 km from Chandigarh and 77 km from Shimla, which makes it one of the easiest hill escapes from the plains.

Monkey Point, the Hanuman temple in the Air Force Station near the Lower Mall, is about 4 km from the town centre. The Solan hills are mild all year — summers rarely pass 32°C and winters seldom drop below 5°C.

how_to_reach.text:
By rail: Kalka is the nearest broad-gauge station.

By road: Chandigarh is about 58 km away; buses run between Solan and Delhi, Chandigarh and Shimla.
